title: Electrically Safe Work Condition & Energized Work Permits

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Electrical room with a 480 V lighting distribution panel and its feeder disconnect; crew of two with LOTO kit, rated meter, PPE. Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Job Mindset: Establishing an ESWC on a 480 V Feeder
scenes.says: Job Mindset for de-energizing a 480-volt feeder. Hazards: shock, arc flash, and back-feeds you didn't find. De-energizing is elimination, the top of the hierarchy. Before you leave the shop, pull current drawings, pack locks and tags for every source, a rated meter with a known source, and the PPE for that equipment. Plan who restricts access. Think ahead: what if there's a generator or UPS tie?

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny facing camera in the electrical room.
scenes.says: NFPA 70E requires an electrically safe work condition before you work inside the limited approach boundary, or interact with equipment where arc-flash likelihood goes up, unless energized work is justified. Here's the process, step by step.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Senior tech checks single-line drawing and panel tags; camera pans to a generator transfer switch label. Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: 1. Find ALL sources: generators, UPS, PV, tie breakers, other control power, capacitors
scenes.says: Step one: determine every possible source of supply. Check up-to-date drawings and identification tags. Look for back-feeds: generators, UPS, PV, tie breakers, control power from other panels, capacitors.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Senior tech in PPE interrupts load, opens the disconnect, looks through the viewing window at open blades.
scenes.on_screen:
2. Interrupt load, open the disconnect
3. Visually verify blades open
scenes.says: Step two: after properly interrupting the load current, open the disconnecting device for each source. Step three: wherever possible, visually verify all blades are fully open, or draw-out breakers are withdrawn to the fully disconnected position.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Senior tech applies lock and tag; then tests with a meter on a known source, each phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground, then the known source again.
scenes.on_screen:
4. Release stored energy
5. Apply LOTO
6. Test: phase-to-phase & phase-to-ground, live-dead-live
7. Ground if induced voltage possible
scenes.says: Step four: release stored energy, like capacitors. Step five: apply lockout/tagout per our policy. Step six: with an adequately rated meter, test each phase, phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground, checking the meter on a known source before and after: live-dead-live. Step seven: where induced voltage or stored energy is possible, ground the conductors before touching them. Until verified, it's energized, and the tester wears the PPE.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny facing camera; on-screen two justifications plus the under-50 V note.
scenes.on_screen:
Energized work only for: Greater hazard • Infeasibility (or under 50 V)
NOT: inconvenience, schedule, customer preference
scenes.says: Energized work is permitted only with a justification. Greater hazard: de-energizing creates more risk, like life-support or alarm systems. Infeasibility: the task can't be done de-energized, like troubleshooting that needs power. Under 50 volts may not need de-energizing. 'The customer doesn't want the lights off' is not a justification. That work gets scheduled after hours.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Table in the electrical room; supervisor and senior tech fill out a printed EEWP form, pen in hand.
scenes.on_screen:
EEWP: circuit & location • work • justification • safe practices
shock assessment • arc-flash assessment • access control
job briefing • approval signatures
scenes.says: When justified energized work crosses the restricted boundary or involves an arc-flash hazard, it goes on a written energized electrical work permit. It covers the circuit and location, the work, the justification, safe work practices, the shock and arc-flash assessment results, how unqualified people are kept out, evidence of a job briefing, and approval signatures. Lesson 5 covers our own form.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny beside a panel with barricade tape and an attendant.
scenes.on_screen:
No permit needed for testing, troubleshooting, voltage measuring
Still need risk assessments, PPE and safe practices
scenes.says: Qualified persons don't need a permit for testing, troubleshooting and voltage measuring, or for thermography and visual inspections that don't cross the restricted boundary. But those tasks still need the shock and arc-flash assessments, PPE and safe work practices. They're exempt only from the paperwork.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Crew in a circle for a job briefing; then cut to Danny.
scenes.on_screen: Scope changes? STOP, back out, reassess
scenes.says: Real-world example from the lesson: a failed breaker in a hospital panel feeding ICU receptacles. The first answer is a planned, coordinated outage. Only if engineering and clinical staff decide de-energizing is the greater hazard does it go to a permit. And if the scope changes mid-task, like a breaker that won't release or damaged bus, stop, back out and reassess.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson and take the quiz
scenes.says: De-energize first, verify every source, and never let convenience justify live work. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Procedure demo: senior technician performs ESWC steps on a 480 V feeder (training gear or a scheduled outage), presenter voice-over. Show live-dead-live clearly and phase-to-phase plus phase-to-ground tests. Do not show actual energized work; the EEWP segment is paperwork and briefing only. Props: single-line drawing, LOTO kit, rated meter with known source, arc-rated PPE, printed generic EEWP form.
